description: Default parameter CSV/TOML data correctness: envelope materials, boundaries, HVAC curves, WH defaults, EV profiles, generators, ZIP parameters, ASHRAE 152 data, and schedules.

reviews.title: Envelope Materials.csv: Resistance and Capacitance vs ASHRAE HOF 2021 Ch.26 Table 4
reviews.prompt: Envelope Materials.csv defines thermal properties for all construction materials. Verify: (a) Resistance (m²·K/W) for each material matches ASHRAE Handbook of Fundamentals 2021 Chapter 26 Table 4. This table provides R-values per unit thickness for common building materials. For layered materials (e.g., gypsum board, plywood, fiberglass batt), verify the thickness column is correct and the total R-value = R_per_unit * thickness matches the table. (b) Capacitance (kJ/m²·K) for each material: ASHRAE HOF Ch.26 provides density, specific heat, and thickness; capacitance = density * specific_heat * thickness / 1000 (for kJ). Verify these derived values are correct—a common error is using volumetric specific heat instead of areal, or incorrect unit conversion from BTU/ft²·°F to kJ/m²·K. (c) Cross-reference boundary names: each material is associated with one or more boundary types (e.g., 'Wood Stud Wall' uses 'Gypsum Board' + 'Fiberglass Batt' + 'OSB Sheathing'). Verify that material names referenced in Boundaries.csv exist in Materials.csv with no typos. (d) Check for missing common materials: XPS foam, polyiso, spray foam (open-cell and closed-cell), concrete (various densities), wood studs, metal studs, carpet, hardwood flooring, asphalt shingles. Missing materials cause fallback to incorrect defaults. (e) Verify that the material list covers the HPXML material vocabulary—if HPXML specifies 'R-13 fiberglass batt' but the CSV only lists 'R-11', the lookup will fail silently.

reviews.title: Envelope Boundaries.csv and Boundary Types.csv: zone labels, assembly R-values
reviews.prompt: Envelope Boundaries.csv defines thermal enclosure assemblies (wall, roof, floor, foundation) and Boundary Types.csv defines boundary condition types. Verify: (a) Zone label mappings: each boundary must be assigned to the correct thermal zone pair (e.g., 'Living Zone <-> Attic', 'Living Zone <-> Ground', 'Living Zone <-> Ambient'). Verify that all possible zone adjacency pairs are covered and that the zone names match those used in the thermal solver. A mismatch would cause the boundary to be assigned to the wrong conduction path. (b) Assembly R-values: each boundary assembly (e.g., 'R-13 Wood Stud Wall') has a total U-factor or R-value. Verify these are computed correctly from the constituent materials (Materials.csv) with correct series/parallel path weighting for framing factor (typically 15-25% framing). ASHRAE parallel-path method: U_assembly = framing_fraction * U_framing + (1 - framing_fraction) * U_cavity. Check that the framing factor default (if present) is reasonable. (c) All HPXML boundary types must have entries: HPXML defines Wall, Roof, Floor, Foundation Wall, Slab, Rim Joist, Door, Window, Skylight. Verify each HPXML type has at least one default entry in Boundaries.csv. A missing HPXML type would crash assembly for dwellings using that type. (d) Window boundary defaults: U-factor and SHGC defaults by climate zone (per IECC). Verify SHGC ranges: 0.25-0.40 for cold climates (passive solar benefit), 0.20-0.30 for hot climates (reduce cooling load). (e) Verify that the boundary CSV does not assign the same material to both sides of an assembly (e.g., gypsum board both as interior finish and as exterior sheathing), which would be physically unrealistic.

reviews.title: HVAC Multispeed Parameters.csv: capacity fractions, EIR curves, fan power
reviews.prompt: HVAC Multispeed Parameters.csv provides speed-dependent performance data for multi-speed and variable-speed HVAC equipment. Verify: (a) Speed-stage capacity fractions: for an N-speed unit, the capacity fractions f_i (i=1..N) should satisfy f_1 ≤ f_2 ≤ ... ≤ f_N = 1.0 (rated speed has fraction 1.0). Common values: 2-speed units have f₁ ≈ 0.67-0.70, f₂ = 1.0; variable-speed units have 5-10 speeds with f₁ ≈ 0.25-0.40, f_N = 1.0. Verify fractions are physically plausible for each equipment category. (b) EIR (energy input ratio) curves: EIR = 1/COP, so cooling EIR should be less than 1.0 (COP > 1). Lower speeds typically have lower EIR (higher COP) due to larger effective heat exchanger area per unit capacity. Verify EIR values decrease as speed decreases. (c) Fan power fractions: fan power typically scales with ~speed³ (cube law) for constant-air-volume systems. Verify fan power fractions are consistent with the cube law for each speed stage. (d) Cross-equipment consistency: a 'high-efficiency 2-speed heat pump' category should have better numbers than a 'standard-efficiency single-speed AC'. Verify categories are clearly labeled and do not mix incompatible parameter sets. (e) Missing categories: check that all HVAC equipment types supported in the codebase have entries—if a code path references a multi-speed curve but the CSV has no entry for that equipment type, the lookup will fail. (f) Verify that the CSV values at rated conditions produce EIR and capacity fraction of exactly 1.0—non-unity values at rated conditions indicate an incorrect reference point that will bias all computations.

reviews.title: Water heating defaults: UEF values, tank volumes, UA values, schedules
reviews.prompt: Water heating default data files. Verify: (a) WH Medium UEF Schedule.csv: UEF values by fuel type and tank size category. Current federal efficiency standards (effective 2015, updated 2023): gas storage ≥ 0.64 UEF for 50-gal, ≥ 0.59 for larger sizes. Electric storage ≥ 0.93 UEF for 50-gal. Heat pump WH ≥ 3.30-3.70 UEF. Verify the CSV values match current DOE standards—outdated values from pre-2015 EF ratings would overestimate performance. (b) default_paramters.csv (note: filename may have typo 'paramters' vs 'parameters'): tank volumes, UA values, recovery efficiencies, setpoints. Verify tank volumes match market-common sizes: 30, 40, 50, 65, 80 gallons (114, 151, 189, 246, 303 L). UA values should scale with surface area: for typical residential tanks with R-10 to R-16 insulation, UA = 1.0-2.0 W/K. Verify UA per unit surface area is consistent across tank sizes. (c) Schedule multipliers: typical hot water draw profiles have morning peak (6-9 AM), evening peak (5-9 PM), and low usage overnight. Average daily hot water draw: ~240 L/day (64 gal/day) for a family of four per ASHRAE. Verify the schedule multiplier integration equals the average daily draw. (d) EnergyPlus uses separate setpoint schedules for different day types (weekday, weekend); verify HARES default schedule format matches this or documents the difference. (e) Check for unit consistency: if UA is specified in W/K in one file and BTU/(h·°F) in another, verify the conversion is applied. A common error is mixing SI and IP units across CSV files.

reviews.title: EV Profiles.csv and per-vehicle/per-level CSVs vs EVI-Pro and DOE data
reviews.prompt: EV default data CSV files under defaults/ev/. Verify all EV profile data against external references: (a) EV Profiles.csv: master list of vehicle types with charging specifications. Verify each vehicle's battery capacity, onboard charger power, and efficiency match EVI-Pro (EVERMI) vehicle database or fueleconomy.gov data. The EVI-Pro model by NREL is the standard for EV charging load modeling. (b) Per-vehicle CSV files: each vehicle type may have its own detailed profile. Verify that the per-vehicle data is internally consistent with the master Profiles.csv and that no vehicles are orphaned (in master list but missing per-vehicle file, or vice versa). (c) Per-charging-level CSV files: Level 1 (120V, 12-16A, 1.44-1.92 kW) and Level 2 (240V, 16-80A, 3.8-19.2 kW) charging profiles. Verify the charging power levels match typical residential EVSE capabilities—most residential L2 is 32A/7.7 kW. The charging efficiency by level: L1 ~85-90% (higher relative overhead), L2 ~90-95%. (d) Range of driving patterns: verify the profiles cover a diverse range: short-range commuter (10-30 mi/day), medium-range commuter (30-60 mi/day), long-range driver (60+ mi/day), weekend-only driver, fleet vehicle, stay-at-home/low-usage. Each profile should have realistic arrival time, departure time, and daily mileage distributions. (e) Verify CSV formatting: consistent column headers, no missing values at critical rows, proper date/time formats if applicable. A CSV parse error in a defaults file can silently load zero values for an entire season of simulation.

reviews.title: Generator efficiency curves: match typical residential backup generator performance
reviews.prompt: Generator default efficiency curve data under defaults/generator/. Verify: (a) Efficiency vs part-load curves: residential backup generators (typically 7-22 kW natural gas or propane) have efficiency curves that peak at 80-100% load with significant drop-off at low part-load. Typical full-load electrical efficiency: 20-25% for small air-cooled engines, 25-30% for liquid-cooled. At 25% part-load, efficiency drops to 15-20%. Verify the curve shape is physically consistent—efficiency should be zero at zero load (no free energy) and should increase monotonically at low loads before plateauing. (b) Fuel consumption at no-load (idle): generators consume ~30-50% of full-load fuel at zero electrical output (idle). This idle consumption drives economics for part-load operation. Verify the no-load fuel consumption value (if present) matches manufacturer spec sheets for Generac, Kohler, or Cummins residential units. (c) Efficiency curve format: verify the independent variable (part-load fraction, kW output, or % rated) is clearly documented and used consistently in the Rust parser. A common error is the curve using fraction [0,1] but the parser expecting percent [0,100]. (d) Multiple generator types: if the CSV covers multiple generator classes (portable, standby, prime power), verify each has distinct curves—a portable generator has much lower efficiency and life than a standby unit. (e) Verify that the curve's maximum output (100% load point) matches the rated capacity column in the same file—mismatched capacity would shift the entire efficiency curve.

reviews.title: ZIP load parameters: Z, I, P coefficients and reactive power defaults
reviews.prompt: ZIP load parameters define constant impedance (Z), constant current (I), and constant power (P) fractions for each load type. Verify: (a) For each load type, Z + I + P = 1.0 (the three fractions must sum to unity). If they don't, the load model is over- or under-determined. Common values: resistive heating (Z=1, I=0, P=0), induction motors (Z=0.2, I=0.3, P=0.5), electronic loads (Z=0, I=0, P=1 for constant-power). Verify assigned values match physical load characteristics. (b) Reactive power defaults: most entries have zero reactive power. This is physically unrealistic for motor loads—induction motors in refrigerators, compressors, and fans have power factors of 0.6-0.85 meaning reactive power is 40-75% of real power. Zero reactive power is reasonable for resistive loads (electric WH, resistance heat, incandescent lighting) but wrong for motor loads. Verify that motor loads (refrigerator, AC compressor, furnace blower, pool pump) have appropriate power factor values, or at minimum that zero reactive power is documented as a known limitation. (c) Verify the TOML file is valid and parseable—TOML syntax errors would cause Rust's toml crate to fail at config load time. (d) Check for voltage exponent parameters: some ZIP models use separate exponents for real and reactive power. Verify the model in the code matches the TOML schema—if code expects exponents but TOML provides fractions, the conversion must be correct. (e) Frequency sensitivity parameters: ZIP models sometimes include df/dP frequency dependence. Verify if this is in the TOML and whether the code uses it.

reviews.title: ASHRAE 152 climate and zone temperature CSVs vs normative data
reviews.prompt: ASHRAE Standard 152 provides normative data for residential energy distribution system efficiency calculations. Verify: (a) ASHRAE152_climate_data.csv: station design temperatures (heating 99.6% and cooling 0.4% dry-bulb and wet-bulb) for representative locations. Cross-reference these against the ASHRAE HOF 2021 Chapter 14 climatic design conditions table. The 99.6% heating design temperature is the temperature exceeded 99.6% of annual hours (the coldest 35 hours per year). The 0.4% cooling design temperature is the temperature exceeded 0.4% of annual hours. Verify these values are correctly labeled—swapping 99.6% and 0.4% columns would produce wrong design day simulations. (b) ASHRAE152_zone_temperatures.csv: default zone temperatures for heating (typically 20-22°C / 68-72°F) and cooling (typically 23.5-25°C / 74-77°F) thermostat setpoints by building type. Verify these match ASHRAE 55 thermal comfort ranges. (c) Verify that the climate zones in the CSV match the IECC climate zone numbering (1A through 8) and that the representative city for each zone is correctly identified. (d) Check for missing climate zones—all 15+ IECC zones should have representative station data. A missing zone would cause failure when simulating dwellings in that zone. (e) Verify unit consistency: if temperatures are in °C in one file and °F in another, the parser must handle the conversion or the files must be consistent. Mixing °C and °F without conversion produces extreme temperature errors (e.g., interpreting 72°F as 72°C).

reviews.title: Default Schedule Parameters.csv: schedule types, seasonal multipliers, patterns
reviews.prompt: Default Schedule Parameters.csv provides fallback schedules when HPXML or user config does not specify them. Verify: (a) All schedule types have defaults: occupancy, lighting, appliance, hot water draw, HVAC thermostat (heating and cooling), ventilation, and any other schedule-driven model. A missing schedule type would cause a silent default of zero or a panic during simulation. (b) Seasonal multipliers: occupancy and internal gain schedules should have seasonal variation—summer vs winter thermostat setpoints (typically 2-3°C higher in summer, lower in winter for energy savings). Verify seasonal multipliers are applied correctly and not inverted. (c) Weekday/weekend patterns: typical patterns have weekday occupancy low during 9 AM - 5 PM (work hours) and high in evenings; weekend occupancy high all day. Verify distinct weekday and weekend patterns are defined. (d) Dwell period vs typical residential occupancy: ASHRAE 90.2/HERS reference home assumes occupancy from 5 PM to 8 AM on weekdays and all day on weekends. Verify the default schedule approximates this pattern with appropriate granularity (hourly or sub-hourly). (e) Morning and evening peaks: hot water draw and appliance usage have characteristic morning peak (6-9 AM) and evening peak (5-9 PM). Verify the schedule shapes capture these peaks with realistic magnitudes. (f) Check CSV formatting: column headers, missing values, date/time format. If the schedule uses a fractional-day format (0.0-1.0 representing 12:00 AM to 12:00 AM), verify the lookup function handles the fractional representation correctly, especially around midnight wrap.
